summary: Degrees are taught as a unit angle: one degree is the angle made by cutting a full turn (a whole circle of rotation) into 360 equal parts, and an angle's measure is the number of one-degree angles it turns through (90° = 90 one-degree angles = a right angle, 180° = half turn, 360° = full turn). This mirrors measuring length and area by iterating a unit, and should precede protractor use so the protractor does not become a meaningless ritual. The activity most directly aimed at building the felt one-degree count has the child sweep a rotating ray and watch a one-degree count accumulate; benchmark images (pattern blocks, clock, compass) and static diagrams support the idea; written response formats (matching, selection, fill-in) can check it.
misconceptions: Thinks a degree measures length, arc length, or the number of tick marks rather than an amount of turn
Sees 360 as arbitrary — no sense that it is the count of equal parts of a full turn — so 90°/180° aren't connected to quarter/half turns
Doesn't see a degree as itself a tiny angle that can be counted and added — treats the number as a label read off a tool
Believes the degree count changes if the arms are drawn longer (arm-length trap carried into measurement)

activities.title: Sweep a ray and count degrees of turn
steps: Grab a ray at the centre of a circle and sweep it round, watching a counter tick up one degree at a time as a thin wedge fills in behind the moving ray.
Notice the rim glow and snap at a quarter turn (90°), half turn (180°), three-quarter turn (270°) and full turn (360°).
Carry out the task 'turn through 45 degrees' and watch 45 little one-degree wedges stack up into half of a right angle.
Make the ray longer and check that the degree count does not change.
activities.insight: A degree is a tiny angle you can count: 90° literally means ninety one-degree turns, and measuring an angle is counting how many one-degree turns it makes — just like measuring length with a tiny unit. Stretching the arms longer leaves the count unchanged.

activities.title: Partition a full turn and name the one-degree angle
steps: Look at a circle of rotation partitioned into equal parts and mark off a quarter, a half and the whole.
Name 1/360 of the full turn as the one-degree angle, and state 90° = quarter turn, 180° = half turn, 360° = whole turn.
Answer: 'What fraction of a full turn is 180°? And 45°?' and 'Why is a full turn 360° and not, say, 100° — what would change if we cut the circle into 100 equal parts instead?'
activities.insight: Choosing 360 parts is a convention (handy because 360 divides evenly by many numbers), but once chosen it fixes the unit: a degree is one of 360 equal parts of a full turn, so each benchmark degree is a definite fraction of a turn (90° = 1/4, 180° = 1/2, 45° = 1/8).

activities.title: Build and combine benchmark angles with pattern blocks
steps: Fit six 60° triangular pattern blocks around a single point and check they close up to a full turn (6 × 60° = 360°).
Use the blocks and a clock/compass image to fix mental pictures of 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, 180° and 360°.
Place a 30° angle and a 60° angle side by side at a point, sharing an arm without overlapping, and state how many degrees altogether, and explain how you know.
activities.insight: Angle measure is additive: decomposed adjacent angles add to the whole (30° + 60° = 90°), and benchmark degrees can be held as mental images before any precise measuring.

activities.title: Check understanding with varied response formats
steps: Match each benchmark to its turn: 90° to a quarter turn, 180° to a half turn, 360° to a whole turn.
Choose what one degree is: 1/360 of a full turn (not a length, not a number of tick marks).
Complete 'a 45° angle has turned through ___ one-degree angles' and explain the answer.

Predict-then-check: shown a right angle with short arms, predict how many degrees it becomes if both arms are extended much longer and say why, before the arms are extended or a long-armed right angle is overlaid vertex-aligned.
activities.insight: The learner can state and apply the definition independently: one degree is 1/360 of a full turn, 45° is 45 one-degree angles, and arm length does not change the amount of turn.

checkQuestion: Show a right angle drawn with short arms and a right angle drawn with long arms. Ask: 'How many degrees is each — is one more than the other, or are they the same?' Then: 'Tell me what one degree actually means.'
checkAnswer: Both are 90° and equal, because arm length does not change the amount of turn; and one degree is 1/360 of a full turn — one of 360 equal parts of a whole rotation, a tiny angle you count — so 90° is 90 of them.
